study.title: Proverbs 24 - Wisdom practice, justice and diligence
study.overview: This chapter brings together sapiential orientations on how the fair should think, speak and act in contrast to the perverse and lazy. He begins by warning against envying the evildoers, begins to show that wisdom, understanding and knowledge sustain personal and social life, insists on the responsibility of assisting the innocent and treating others with justice, and ends with a vivid image of the ruin caused by laziness. The notes indicate that the final section continues the collection of the "dicts of the wise" and adds more proverbs to this set.

outline.title: Do not envy the wicked; wisdom builds
outline.explanation: The opening forbids desire company or lifestyle of evil men, because their interior produces destruction and oppression. Then wisdom, understanding, and knowledge appear as foundations of the house, that is, of life and of the family, bringing stability and provision.

outline.title: Force, advice and duty to save the innocent
outline.explanation: Wisdom strengthens man, and prudent decisions require many counsels. Then the chapter calls the wise man to act on the day of anguish, including defending those who are led to death, for God weighs the hearts and repays to each one according to his works.

outline.title: Sweet wisdom, perseverance of the righteous and fear of the LORD
outline.explanation: Wisdom is compared to honey: pleasurable and beneficial for the soul. The text teaches that the righteous one can fall and rise, while the wicked stumbles in evil; it also forbids to rejoice at the fall of the enemy. The section concludes with the call to fear the LORD and the king, avoiding joining the rebels, whose ruin will come suddenly.

outline.title: Justice in the trial and the end of laziness
outline.explanation: The final proverbs deal with impartiality in court, the correct answer to others, the diligent planning of work and the refusal to repay evil with evil. The chapter ends with the observation of the lazy field, taken by thorns and the fallen wall, showing that a little sloppy produces rapid and inevitable poverty.

study.context: Tyndale's notes say that 24:23-34 continues the so-called Trintic of the Wise (22:17-24:22) and adds five more sayings. The section on the lazy, according to Tyndale and Adam Clarke, is a lesson observed in practice, and Matthew Henry's note relates it to diligence and prudent administration of domestic life. This material does not authorize more specific historical details than this.
study.theology: The chapter presents wisdom as something moral and spiritual, not only intellectual: it builds life, guides decisions, sustains justice and produces perseverance. The fear of the LORD appears as the axis of correct conduct, together with respect for legitimate authority. There is also a theology of responsibility before God: He knows hearts, sees omission before injustice, and repays according to works. In addition, the text shows that the righteous one is not defined by never falling, but by rising, while perversity self-destroys. Biblical wisdom therefore unites prudence, prudence, compassion, impartiality, and diligent work.

scholarViews.insight: Wisdom requires an active stance against injustice: the wise do what they can to prevent oppression and suffering.
It is not to envy sinners or desire their condition, because their way is already corrupted in the heart and acting.
Theemer to the Lord and to the king link the true religion to civil allegiance; authentic piety cannot be separated from fidelity to the legitimate authorities.

questions: In what situations have I desired, even though secretly, the apparent freedom of the wicked rather than seeking the wisdom of God?
Is there anyone at risk, oppressed or wronged in my power to whom I should help with words, defense or concrete action?
Does my routine reveal diligence and planning, or does it look more like an abandoned field, where small neglects produce large losses?
study.practice: This week, choose a concrete area to practice Proverbs 24: organize a postponed task, ask wise people advice before an important decision and examine whether there is any act of injustice, omission or revenge that needs to be abandoned. In addition, take time to encourage and protect someone vulnerable, rather than just observing your need. The chapter calls the believer to replace envy with fear of the LORD, laziness with diligence and indifference for justice.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are in English and, in some excerpts, appear truncated; therefore, the above observations are strictly limited to what was explicitly said in them. It is not safe to affirm historical, geographical, archaeological or linguistic details beyond what the notes support. It is also not possible to ensure a complete reconstruction of Matthew Henry's interpretation in verses whose excerpt came cut.
